tasks.short: Find suitable training, get paid courses approved, register and block the days, attend, and record certificates.

steps.what: Substitute teacher searches course and workshop listings that fit their needs
Substitute pool coordinator approves paid training
Substitute teacher registers and blocks the days in the cover calendar
Substitute teacher attends the training workshops or conferences
Substitute teacher files certificates and hours in a personal portfolio

tasks.design: The substitute pool's {LMS} lists approved courses with filters and an approval request to the pool coordinator; once approved, registration blocks the days in the cover {CALENDAR}, and completed courses land in the substitute's portfolio with certificate. Attending stays as it is.
tasks.previous_blocker: Courses were found one by one and certificates kept in folders.
tasks.enabler_now: Learning systems hold course catalogues, approval flows and completion records.
tasks.still_hard: Learning happens in the room; the catalogue only helps if the pool keeps it current.
tasks.human_edge: Choosing what to learn next from what went wrong in last week's classes.
tasks.altitude: Nothing changes in decision rights; admin around training shrinks.

reach.task: Plan training for the substitute pool
reach.learn: Whether the catalogue shows gaps in the pool's skills.

evidence.claim: Learning systems hold course catalogues, approval flows and completion records.
A firm with a works council needs consent for rules on staff data.

assumptions: Boundary: from finding training to recording it; the course content is outside.
Input contract: course catalogue and approval rules kept by the pool coordinator; fallback is search and e-mail.
Coordinator time is outside the substitute's savings.
unknowns: Whether the substitute works through a pool with a learning system.
research_questions: Does the catalogue raise uptake of training among substitutes?

incremental.description: Substitute teacher keeps the portfolio profile current.

approvals.approved_version: The course, dates and cost as approved by the pool coordinator in s2; another course or date needs a new approval.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Substitutes outside a pool, or with few training days, save little.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Pick games for the group and space, get the equipment, explain rules, supervise play and report broken equipment.

steps.what: Substitute teacher picks games that suit the group and the space
Substitute teacher fetches the equipment from the storeroom
Substitute teacher explains the rules and forms teams
Substitute teacher supervises games and recreational play and settles disputes
Substitute teacher tidies up and tells the caretaker about broken equipment

tasks.design: A short games card set in {DOCS}, sorted by age, group size and space, helps the substitute choose, and broken equipment is reported through the school's facilities form instead of hunting for the caretaker. Explaining, supervising and settling disputes stay in person.
tasks.previous_blocker: Substitutes chose games from memory and reported damage by word of mouth.
tasks.enabler_now: Shared card sets and simple report forms are easy to set up.
tasks.still_hard: Running games for an unknown group is about presence and fairness.
tasks.human_edge: Making sure every child gets a turn and nobody is left out.
tasks.altitude: Nothing changes; choosing and reporting are quicker.

reach.task: Keep the games card set current

evidence.claim: Shared card sets and facilities report forms are simple school tools.

assumptions: Boundary: from picking games to equipment reported; repairs are outside.
Input contract: games card set kept by the physical education teacher; facilities form run by the caretaker; fallback is memory and word of mouth.
Caretaker time is outside the substitute's savings.
research_questions: Do substitutes pick more varied games with the card set?

incremental.description: Substitute teacher reads the card set before the session.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Experienced substitutes pick games by habit and save almost nothing.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Check the bus list, help children board and exit, count them, and report anyone missing.

steps.what: Substitute teacher checks the paper bus list for which children travel today
Substitute teacher helps students boarding the school buses
Substitute teacher counts children and ticks them off on the list
Substitute teacher helps children exit and hands them to staff or parents
Substitute teacher phones the office about a missing child

tasks.design: Today's bus list, with absences already removed, opens on the substitute's phone from the student information system ({OTHER}) and children are ticked off there, so the office sees who boarded. Helping children on and off and calling about a missing child stay as they are.
tasks.previous_blocker: Bus lists were printed in the morning and did not show late absences.
tasks.enabler_now: Pupil records systems hold attendance and can show lists on phones with role-based access.
tasks.still_hard: Safety at the bus depends entirely on attention; phones must not distract.
tasks.human_edge: Noticing the child who is not where they should be.
tasks.altitude: Nothing changes; the list is current and shared.

reach.task: Track which children travelled by bus
reach.learn: Whether shared tick-off ends end-of-day phone checks.

evidence.claim: Records apps with role-based access can show today's lists on a phone.
Children's data must be limited to what the task needs and protected under the GDPR.

assumptions: Boundary: from checking the list to children handed over; transport contracts are outside.
Input contract: bus list and absences kept by the school administrator in the system; short-term access for the substitute; fallback is the printed list.
Office time is outside the substitute's savings.
Boarding help and missing-child calls do not change.
unknowns: Whether the school runs its own buses.
research_questions: Do late absences cause fewer false alarms with a live list?

incremental.description: Substitute teacher logs in and learns the tick-off screen.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Small buses with a few known children need little list work.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Mark closed and open questions with the teacher's key and rubric, total and convert scores, add comments, and post grades after the teacher releases them.

steps.what: Substitute teacher collects the work, answer key and rubric
Substitute teacher marks closed questions in students' exams against the key by hand
Substitute teacher marks open answers and assignments with the rubric
Substitute teacher records each rubric score by clicking it in the test tool
Substitute teacher adds up points and converts them to grades
Substitute teacher writes short feedback comments on each piece
Regular teacher checks and releases the grades
Substitute teacher types the grades into the student information system

tasks.design: Tests set up in the school's digital test tool mark closed items against the regular teacher's key; open answers are scored by the substitute with a click rubric and a comment bank, and points convert to grades by the school's formula. After the regular teacher releases the grades, they post to the student information system ({OTHER}); no model scores or comments on pupils' work, which keeps this outside high-risk AI.
tasks.previous_blocker: Closed items were marked by hand and totals were added in spreadsheets.
tasks.enabler_now: Digital test tools auto-mark closed items and export grades; rubric forms compute scores.
tasks.still_hard: Paper tests still need hand marking; judging open answers is the core skill, and AI that evaluates learning outcomes would be high-risk.
tasks.human_edge: Seeing what a pupil meant in a messy answer and writing a comment that helps.
tasks.altitude: The substitute marks only what needs judgement; grade release stays with the regular teacher.

reach.task: Set up tests and rubrics in the test tool
reach.learn: Whether shared keys make cover marking consistent.

evidence.claim: Digital test tools mark closed items against a key and export grades.
AI that evaluates learning outcomes in educational institutions at all levels is high-risk.
High-risk obligations for education AI apply from 2 December 2027.

assumptions: Boundary: from collecting work to grades posted; appeals are outside.
Input contract: answer key, rubric and grade formula set up in the test tool by the regular teacher; pupils take closed parts digitally; fallback is hand marking.
Regular teacher time is outside the substitute's savings.
research_questions: Do substitute-marked grades differ from the regular teacher's on the same work?

already_counted.description: Substitute teacher checks auto-marked items with unusual answers.

incremental.description: Substitute teacher handles test tool access issues.
Regular teacher sets up keys and rubrics in the test tool.

approvals.approved_version: The grade list as released by the regular teacher in s7; any change needs a new release.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Subjects tested mostly on paper or with open answers keep most marking time.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The substitute keeps teaching, supervising and judging work; lists, bookings and closed-item marking move to shared systems.
skills_to_grow: Working in a school's systems with short-term access
role.ambitious_version: A substitute who marks only what needs judgement and is never missing a list or a key.
